title: The Rise of the Championship “Gap Year”
subtitle: The Kansas City Chiefs and Florida Panthers are betting that one lost season doesn’t have to close a title window — especially when the stars and structure of the dynasty remain intact.
contentHtml:
This month, two recent dynasties are embarking on similar return-trip journeys that, until recently, didn’t exactly have a huge amount of precedent for success.

Subscribe now

Prior to 2025, the Kansas City Chiefs had gone to seven consecutive AFC championship games (2018-2024), making five Super Bowls in that span and winning three of them. The dynasty had gone through serious changes over the course of those seven seasons, starting out as an all-offense/no-defense squad before eventually flipping around to be something like the opposite — if not quite as extreme — by the end. But they still specialized in winning games… until they didn’t anymore, that is, crashing out to 6-11 last season with Patrick Mahomes getting injured as well.

Over in the NHL, the Florida Panthers underwent their own extreme evolution, from a historically offensive-minded squad to one built around toughness and defense as much or more than scoring firepower. It worked wonders as Florida went to three consecutive Stanley Cup Finals from 2023-2025, winning the latter two to join the 2016/17 Penguins and 2020/21 Lightning as the NHL’s only back-to-back champs since 1998. But last year’s Cats were the most injured team in the league, cratering to a 40-42 record and missing the playoffs.

Both teams are now trying to turn those down-years into one-off blips in otherwise dominant multi-year résumés — and it might work, if the market forecasts are any indication. K.C. began their path back to the top on Monday night, easily beating the rival Broncos despite Patrick Mahomes posting the third-worst single-game CPOE of his career (-11.9%). Meanwhile, the Panthers’ trek will begin at their own rival, the defending Cup champ Hurricanes, on September 29.

K.C. currently ranks fourth in ’s Super Bowl futures odds, while Florida is tied with Carolina and Colorado for the top spot on the Stanley Cup side:

Traders may not be batting an eye over the concept of a championship window staying open through a down season (or more!) because of the very recent precedent set by Steph Curry and the Golden State Warriors.

After losing the 2019 NBA title in an upset against the Toronto Raptors, the Warriors’ dynasty seemed to fall apart all at once. Kevin Durant, who helped supercharge an already-great squad into arguably the greatest NBA team ever, ruptured his Achilles during the Finals and left the Bay for Brooklyn anyway. Klay Thompson tore his ACL in Game 6 and would miss the following TWO seasons, joining a growing list of veteran absences that even Curry couldn’t escape, after Steph broke his hand four games into the 2019-20 season. With nearly every pillar of their previous run either gone or unavailable, the Warriors fell to an NBA-worst 15-50 record — suffering one of the fastest descents from an all-time great team to the bottom of the league.

Any normal baseline expectations for future success would seem to need resetting from that point… but the Warriors were far from normal. After improving to 39-33 (ultimately losing out in the Play-In) in 2020-21, Golden State returned in full force in 2021-22 — going 53-29 and then storming through the playoffs to defeat the Boston Celtics 4-2 in the NBA Finals, with Curry being named MVP. From that point on, no “gap year” sequence could truly cause a former champion to be written off as long as their winning core was intact on the other side.

(Incidentally, that surprise run may have hurt subsequent versions of the Warriors, since it made it impossible to distinguish between temporary setbacks and legitimate declines that needed a real reset. But hey man, flags fly forever.)

Before those Warriors, there were other franchise arcs that broadly fit the same definition, of a champion team bottoming out to a below-average Elo rating and then returning to win the title again within 5 years:

  • Boston Red Sox, 2013-2018: After winning it all in 2013, Boston immediately fell back to last place in the AL East in both 2014 and 2015 — only to rebuild around a new generation and win 108 games plus another World Series in 2018.

  • Alternating even/odd years of the San Francisco Giants’ 2010s dynasty: The Giants literally mastered the art of the “gap year”, winning championships in 2010, 2012 and 2014 while missing the postseason entirely in both 2011 and 2013.

  • New York Giants, 2007-2011: Eli Manning’s Giants knocked off the Patriots in Super Bowl XLII, drifted out of the playoffs within a few years, then resurfaced from a 9-7 regular season to beat New England again in the sequel four seasons later.

  • St. Louis Cardinals, 2006-2011: The Cardinals followed their unlikely 83-win championship in 2006 with two straight playoff misses — including a 78-84 record in 2007 — before another wild-card team caught fire and won it all in 2011.

  • Washington Redskins, 1987-1991: Fresh off destroying Denver 42-10 in Super Bowl XXII with Doug Williams under center, Washington went 17-15 over the next two seasons with zero playoff trips. But in 1991, this time with Mark Rypien at QB, they returned to championship glory by handing Buffalo its second of four straight SB losses.

  • Minnesota Twins, 1987-1991: Minnesota went from 1987’s champs to three straight non-playoff seasons — posting just 74 wins in 1990 — before going worst-to-first for another title in the legendary 1991 World Series.

  • L.A./Oakland Raiders, 1980-1983: The Raiders won the Super Bowl out of Oakland in 1980, relocated to Los Angeles in 1982, and then returned to the top with another championship in 1983.

  • L.A./Brooklyn Dodgers, 1955-1959: Powered by stars like Duke Snider, Roy Campanella, Johnny Podres and the great Jackie Robinson, Brooklyn finally broke through for their first-ever title in 1955 — then moved across the country three years later, bottomed out in their first L.A. season, and (remarkably) won the World Series again in 1959.

  • St. Louis Cardinals, 1931-1934: After winning 101 games and the World Series in 1931, St. Louis plunged to 72-82 the next year before the “Gashouse Gang” climbed back to the top and won it all again in 1934.

  • New York Yankees, 1923-1927: The Yankees followed the very first of what’s now 27 World Championships with a slide that bottomed out at 69-85 in 1925 — the year of Babe Ruth’s “bellyache” — then rebuilt into the legendary 110-win “Murderers’ Row” champions of 1927.

Of these, some are more akin to what the Chiefs and Panthers are trying to do (and what the Warriors actually pulled off) than others. Many of the teams on our list substantially turned over their rosters in a short period between wins, which is not the same as our “dynasty took a year off” concept.

Others were more mixed, retaining only some of the same stars: Ruth obviously was a N.Y. cornerstone throughout, for instance, but Wally Pipp (NOT Lou Gehrig) started at 1B for the ‘23 Yankees. And again, Joe Gibbs’s Washington teams had different QBs leading Gary Clark, Art Monk, Darrell Green and company. Even the 2006-11 Cardinals had only three players appear in both World Series: Chris Carpenter, Yadier Molina and Albert Pujols.

Perhaps the closest comps are the 2010s baseball Giants, the 2007-11 football Giants, and the early-’80s Raiders — teams with more continuity — but even those are imperfect as parallels. The 2010s Giants were just too damn weird to be like anybody else; Eli Manning would never take a gap-year (famously, he never missed a start throughout most of his tenure with Big Blue); and although Jim Plunkett quarterbacked both Raiders champions, the 1983 version had evolved a lot around him to put greater emphasis on Super Bowl MVP Marcus Allen at RB.

That’s what makes the Chiefs and Panthers such interesting proofs of the concept. Kansas City is still built around Mahomes, Andy Reid, Travis Kelce, Chris Jones and much of the structure that produced three championships. Florida still has Matthew Tkachuk, Paul Maurice and Sam Reinhart, with Sasha Barkov returning from injury and brother Brady Tkachuk joining the mix. In both cases, the bet is essentially that last season only represented a temporary interruption in service.

The Warriors proved that bet can pay off. But the rest of our sample shows how rare it is for a championship core to genuinely bottom out and then simply pick up where it left off again. Usually, by the time a former champ climbs all the way back, enough has changed that we’re really talking about a new team wearing the same laundry. But now the Chiefs and Panthers get to find out whether Golden State truly offered a new blueprint for extending a dynasty’s window through a “gap year” — or if Curry and friends merely produced one of the great exceptions to the rule in championship history.
